title: Kirby's Dream Land
principle: Let players use enemies, not only defeat them
why: He found it fun for the player to use enemies, because of risk and reward and the dual purpose enemies serve; Mega Man's boss weapons are a reward for winning, not using the enemies.
how: Give the player a simple way to turn on-screen enemies into tools, such as inhaling and spitting them out.
example: Kirby's Dream Land inhale (a tongue grab was the first idea) vs. Mega Man boss weapons.
quote: I just thought it would be fun if the player could use enemies.

title: Risk and Reward
principle: Put risk and reward close together, in the right amounts
why: Fun comes from taking risks to get rewards; in Super Mario Bros. the highest-risk moment, right next to the Koopa Troopa, is the only time you can beat it.
how: Design core interactions so the player must enter danger to score, and attach new risk to rewards, like a kicked shell that can bounce back.
anti_pattern: Rewards with no attached risk.
example: Space Invaders: you can only hit an invader from where it can hit you. Super Mario Bros.: stomping a Koopa Troopa, then kicking its shell.
quote: Take risks to get rewards. This push and pull is the very core of game essence.

title: Squeeze and Release
principle: Squeeze players with stress, then release it
why: Stress alone isn't fun, but heavy pressure followed by sudden release brings great satisfaction; a game with no stress probably wouldn't be much fun.
how: Put an enemy, obstacle or puzzle in the way of progress, then let the player overcome it.
anti_pattern: Weeding stress out entirely.
quote: Stress on its own isn't fun, but if you really squeeze a player, then whoosh! set them free, it can bring great satisfaction.

title: Squeeze and Release
principle: Reward cleared challenges with choices that prepare for the next
why: Release is just the first step; rewards should give new ways to relieve stress more effectively, and providing choice boosts game essence.
how: After each challenge, grant EXP, new skills or currency for equipment, and let the player choose how to use them.
anti_pattern: Rewards that are only linear progress with no choice.
example: Experience points, new skills, currency for better equipment.
quote: Apply stress, allow for release, and prepare players for what's next.

title: Kirby's Adventure
principle: Give every enemy a meaning the player looks forward to
why: The copy ability made players look forward to each new enemy encounter, so every individual enemy had meaning, and it boosted Kirby's appeal as a character.
how: Let each enemy type offer something distinct the player can take, such as an ability.
example: Kirby's Adventure copy abilities.
quote: Every individual enemy now had meaning, which was a huge deal.

title: Game Essence in Role-Playing Games
principle: Make going deeper a gamble with spoils at stake
why: In RPG exploration, deeper areas hold stronger enemies but greater rewards, and falling in battle loses the spoils you found, so risk and reward are clear.
how: Scale enemy strength and rewards with dungeon depth and make defeat cost collected spoils so retreating is a real choice.
quote: Do you press your luck? Or get out while you still can?

title: Game Essence in Role-Playing Games
principle: Telegraph enemy weaknesses and reward exploiting them
why: Players size enemies up by look and behavior; exploiting weaknesses is both strategy and game essence, and Persona's weakness combos add variety and rhythm. Casual games shouldn't get too complex.
how: Give enemies cues that hint at weaknesses and reward exploiting them with extra payoffs like combo setups, scaled to your audience.
anti_pattern: Overly complex weakness systems in casual games.
example: Persona: exploiting weaknesses sets up combos.
quote: Exploiting enemy weaknesses to maximize your damage output— that's both strategy and game essence at play.

title: Fun Beyond Game Essence
principle: Identify which source of fun your game relies on beyond game essence.
why: Fun comes from more than push and pull: control feel, story, fandom, simulation, creation and rhythm can each carry a game.
how: Name your game's main source of fun and invest in it; for example, fine-tune control feel if controlling the character is the fun.
anti_pattern: Assuming a compelling story alone is enough to make a good game.
example: Ace Attorney, Animal Crossing, beatmania and a train simulator as fun beyond pure game essence.
quote: Game essence isn't the only thing that makes a game fun

title: Fun Beyond Game Essence
principle: Layer risk and reward onto creation and timing-based play.
why: Crafting is fun on its own, but dangers like falling, enemies or risky gathering can make it a lot more fun; strict timing keeps rhythm games tense.
how: Add fall deaths, enemies that make building defenses matter, or dangerous resource trips; keep timing judgment strict enough that slightly late is a miss.
anti_pattern: Loose judgment that gives Goods or Bads further from the note, reducing risk.
example: beatmania, where a hair late counts as a miss.
quote: there would be less risk involved, and people might find it a bit boring.

title: That Was Then, This Is Now
principle: Judge fun as relative to its time and context.
why: The year you play, your personal situation, trends and technology all greatly affect how much fun a game is.
how: Replay an old game today next to a recent one before deciding which is better.
anti_pattern: Comparing a modern game against your memory of an old one.
quote: The fun of a game isn't based in absolutes. It's more of a relative thing.

title: Let Players Cheat the System
principle: Leave some within-the-rules exploits for players to discover
why: Getting gains without losses is fun and memorable, and players will try to cheat the system anyway; just following the path laid out for them isn't very fun.
how: When testing turns up a balance-breaking trick that stays inside the rules (luring enemies off ledges, farming a rare high-value enemy, resetting for a result), consider keeping it instead of patching it out.
anti_pattern: Removing every exploit during debugging by reflex, or letting players rewrite game parameters.
example: Dark Souls enemies tricked into falling to their deaths; Dragon Quest metal slime farming
quote: it's okay to let players cheat the system just a bit within the bounds of your game.

title: Let Players Cheat the System
principle: Analyze strategy as minimizing losses and maximizing gains
why: Defined this way, strategy applies to every genre with push and pull, and it includes taking a larger loss for an even greater gain.
how: For each system, list the ways players can cut losses, raise gains, and trade a big loss for a bigger gain; make sure meaningful trades exist.
example: Action, FPS, fighting, RPG, RTS, puzzle and gambling games
quote: strategy is how players minimize losses and maximize gains.

title: The Potential of One Button
principle: Build one-button play on timing, reaction, or hold-and-release decisions
why: Rapid tapping is tiring and favors naturally fast tappers, and plain holding has little game essence; deciding when to press, release or let go creates the skill.
how: Ask players to press or release at the right moment (release when the crane lines up), or to alternate (hold to catch eggs, release to avoid bombs).
anti_pattern: Mash-only or hold-only mechanics.
example: Crane Fever, Megaton Punch, Egg Catcher
quote: These games revolve around knowing when to keep the button pressed and when to release.

title: The Potential of One Button
principle: Let reaction games include bluffing so players can fake each other out
why: Pure reflex tests become push and pull once opponents can feint the signal.
how: In head-to-head reaction games, make the start signal something players can imitate or feint, like making the "kah!" sound with their mouths.
example: Quick Draw and multiplayer Samurai Kirby
quote: These games are a test of reflexes, but they allow for push and pull, since players can fake each other out.

title: Deconstruct, Analyze, and Rebuild
principle: Deconstruct why something is fun, then rebuild it originally
why: Copying something fun won't feel original; understanding why it's fun lets you rebuild it into a unique work, and practicing the process deepens your understanding.
how: Deconstruct (pick the fun part, e.g. drifting), analyze (why: risk and reward), then rebuild in a new form (e.g. brake to charge, drift, release for a speed burst).
anti_pattern: Copying a fun game wholesale.
example: Kirby Air Ride's one-button charge drifting
quote: I deconstructed, analyzed, and rebuilt, and that's where I ended up.

title: Deconstruct, Analyze, and Rebuild
principle: Reward risky actions tangibly, after completion, without snowballing
why: A score bonus gives no tangible benefit, permanent power-ups let skilled players run away with it, and some speed is needed so the risk is rewarded.
how: Grant a temporary benefit such as a speed burst once the risky action is done (at the curve's exit), not throughout it.
anti_pattern: Score-only rewards, or permanent power-ups that let skilled players run away with the game.
example: Drifting in Kirby Air Ride
quote: Instead of increasing speed throughout the drift, it's better to increase it after the player clears the curve.

title: Deconstruct, Analyze, and Rebuild
principle: Design for what's fun as a game, not for realism
why: A realistic driving experience leaves little room for creativity; real drifting is slower than grip driving, yet making drifting fun makes the game fun.
how: When realism and fun conflict, side with fun; Sakurai doesn't take cues from his real-world driving hobby.
example: Drifting vs. grip driving
quote: At the end of the day, I design things that I think will be fun as games.

title: Kirby Air Ride
principle: Broaden play styles instead of rewarding a single perfect method
why: Shaving tenths of a second has game essence, but Sakurai wanted a broader design where players don't converge on one method.
how: Add a mode built for variety, such as a large sandbox with differing power-ups and events, so every session plays differently.
anti_pattern: Designing only around perfection and time-shaving.
example: Kirby Air Ride's City Trial
quote: Instead of encouraging perfection, a major concept of the game was expanding the possible play types.

title: Falling Sells the Feeling of Flight
principle: Pair every movement mechanic with an opposing force
why: No motion feels complete without an opposing element; risk and reward are two sides of the same coin, like player and enemy attacks.
how: Give flight a falling mechanic, penalty or requirement to fly, and give high speed conditions that slow players down.
anti_pattern: Adding a mechanic without anything that opposes it.
quote: When you're adding a mechanic to your game, think about how to oppose that mechanic, too.

title: Falling Sells the Feeling of Flight
principle: Put obstacles near flight paths so players can thread the needle
why: The great feeling comes from the inherent risk and the sense of barely scraping by; nothing but sky would have no tension.
how: Place ground, water and structures like bridges near flight routes; add terrain or obstacles to space and high-altitude settings.
anti_pattern: Open sky or space with nothing to crash into.
example: Flying under the long bridge in the first Ace Combat
quote: Imagine a game with nothing but sky, with no ground at all to crash into. It wouldn't have any tension.

title: Falling Sells the Feeling of Flight
principle: Tie superhuman movement to interactions with the environment
why: Flight feels good when the interaction with the surroundings is spot-on; hunting for launch spots is fun, and contrast between fliers and non-fliers adds enjoyment.
how: Trigger flight from cliffs and ramps, and include machines or characters that can and can't fly.
example: Kirby Air Ride flight spots and machines
quote: I'd say you need to get the player's interaction with the surrounding environment absolutely spot-on.

title: Do We Really Need Enemies?
principle: Build every loop as stress, relief, growth, then progress
why: Relief, growth and progress are what make a game fun, but they are hard to establish without initial stress from an obstacle.
how: Map your core loop into the four steps and name what supplies each; add an obstacle, reward or next goal wherever a step is missing.
anti_pattern: Removing obstacles entirely, which removes the relief and growth too.
quote: Stress, relief, growth, and progress.

title: Do We Really Need Enemies?
principle: Replace removed enemies with another source of stress
why: Enemies exist to provide stress and relief; a game without enemies still needs that stress, and extra stress relieved feels extra rewarding.
how: If combat is cut, create stress through characters in peril, indirect obstacles or costs, and reward harder solutions with bigger progress.
anti_pattern: Assuming a no-combat game can work without stress.
example: Undertale's Pacifist route overcomes enemies indirectly, which may be even more stressful and rewarding.
quote: To summarize, it's possible to take enemies out of games if you want, but you still need the stress and relief they provide.

title: Do We Really Need Enemies?
principle: Give every saved-up resource a worthwhile use
why: Paying for things is its own stress and relief: an expensive item lets players save up and look forward to owning it.
how: Pair each resource with things to buy, including at least one expensive goal worth saving toward.
anti_pattern: Infinite resources with no way to use them.
example: A mining game with infinite resources and nothing to use them on would be pointless.
quote: There'd be no point in a mining game where you can get infinite resources but have no way to use them, right?

title: Meteos
principle: Design from the genre's risk and reward, even if you're bad at it
why: He is bad at falling-block puzzles but could still propose Meteos by working out the principles of their game essence: stacking blocks is risk that careful play turns into a big reward.
how: Write your genre's risk and reward in one sentence, then brainstorm other ways to discharge that risk than the default action.
example: Meteos: matched blocks blast off into the air instead of disappearing.
quote: Even though I'm not great at these games, I knew I could come up with a proposal if I just figured out the principles behind their game essence.

title: Consider Rewards First
principle: Design the reward system as soon as the core game works
why: Progress alone doesn't motivate players in modern games; rewards are the source of their investment.
how: Once the bones are in place, list what every enemy, mission and activity grants and where each reward is used.
quote: Rewards are key to keeping players engaged! So like I said earlier, you should make them the first thing you consider.

title: Consider Rewards First
principle: Pair every accumulated currency with appealing things to spend it on
why: Money or points saved over time need a spending outlet, and if what you can buy is unappealing or unsuitable it won't turn out well.
how: Design the spending side alongside the earning side and check each purchasable item is desirable and fits the game.
anti_pattern: Currencies with dull or ill-fitting sinks.
quote: Money or points—numerical rewards you save up over time— should naturally come packaged with a way to spend them.

title: Consider Rewards First
principle: Make crafted items feel like profit and a must-have
why: Turning collected materials into something new is particularly effective, but only if players feel they profit and want the result.
how: Price recipes so the output is clearly worth more than its materials, and make outputs things players actively want.
anti_pattern: Loops where gathering materials is the only thing you do.
quote: It's vital the player feels like they're profiting, and that the end product is a must-have.

title: Consider Rewards First
principle: Grant collectibles as rewards instead of unlocking them at start
why: A collection feature has no joy if everything is available from the beginning.
how: Gate characters, equipment and collection items behind play so each one is earned.
anti_pattern: Unlocking everything from the start.
example: Smash Bros. Ultimate's Spirits would have no joy if unlocked at the start.
quote: In Smash Bros. Ultimate, for example, if we didn't grant Spirits as rewards but had them unlocked at the start, there'd be no joy in the feature.

title: Do Competitive Games Have to Be Complex?
principle: Add mechanics one at a time, each creating new push and pull
why: A fighter with one punch and no walking has no push and pull; walking adds range, and jumping, guarding and throwing each add depth.
how: Start from a minimal core and add one mechanic at a time, writing down the new decision it creates; cut any that create none.
anti_pattern: Rules that add complexity without push and pull.
example: Street Fighter II's moves each had specific roles, giving incredible depth.
quote: Each of these features gradually brings depth to our game.

title: Do Competitive Games Have to Be Complex?
principle: Give stronger moves longer recovery so whiffs can be punished
why: Making the kick recover longer than the punch means a miss can be countered, which is the point where push and pull appears.
how: Pair each move's power with matching recovery so committing to a strong move carries risk.
quote: If we give the kick a longer recovery than the punch so it can be countered if you miss. Well, now we've got some push and pull.

title: Game Essence in Falling-Block Puzzle Games
principle: Design from why an action is fun, not from the action itself
why: Understanding the genre's essence let him come up with Meteos's launching idea in five minutes despite being bad at the genre.
how: Before fixing the core action, write why the genre's usual action is fun and brainstorm other actions that deliver the same payoff.
anti_pattern: Starting from the assumption that blocks have to disappear.
example: Meteos launches blocks instead of erasing them.
quote: You shouldn't start your design with the idea that blocks have to disappear, but instead consider why it's fun to make those blocks disappear.

title: Game Essence in Falling-Block Puzzle Games
principle: Make the biggest rewards require the biggest accumulated risk
why: Taking great risk to clear many blocks at once makes the result feel even better.
how: Tie your largest payoffs to states where the player has let danger build up.
example: Tetris: stacking high is risky, and clearing lots of blocks at once needs that risk.
quote: You need to put yourself at great risk in order to clear lots of blocks at once, which makes the end result feel even better.

title: Game Essence in Falling-Block Puzzle Games
principle: Escalate risk over time to keep tension rising
why: Tetrominos gradually falling faster raises risk and makes the game more exciting.
how: Increase speed or pressure steadily over a session so decisions get harder as play goes on.
example: Tetris pieces speed up as time passes.
quote: The way Tetrominos gradually start falling quicker as time passes also serves to heighten risk, and thus makes the game more exciting.

title: Game Essence in Falling-Block Puzzle Games
principle: Let skilled players cling to life at the edge
why: Letting pieces be rotated and slid after landing lets players cling to life, which invites even greater risk-taking.
how: Add last-moment recovery options so players can push their luck further.
example: Later Tetris ports allowed rotating and sliding pieces after they land.
quote: a significant addition, as being able to cling to life like this invites even greater risk.

title: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking
principle: Carry a proven push-and-pull core into adaptations
why: Mushiking's rock-paper-scissors battles, with each Mushi specializing in one shape, already created push and pull through reading the opponent.
how: When adapting a hit to a new format, keep its tested core interaction and spend design effort on what the new format adds.
example: Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking arcade battles via rock-paper-scissors.
quote: Each Mushi specialized in one of the three shapes, which led to the game's push and pull.

title: Praise the Player!
principle: Praise good plays explicitly, beyond items and progress
why: Games are meant to be fun; items and progress are expected by design and aren't there specifically to tell players they've done well.
how: Add crowd cheers on big launches and KOs, or have allied characters praise the player based on feats like enemies defeated.
anti_pattern: Treating item drops and progression as all the praise a player needs.
example: Smash Bros. crowd cheers on launches, KOs and the victory screen; Dynasty Warriors commanders praise the player based on enemies defeated.
quote: Games are meant to be fun, so it's important to praise players for doing something good.

title: Praise the Player!
principle: Hand out bonuses generously, even when players stumble
why: In Forza, whether you drive great or wreck your car, you still get some kind of bonus; these are praise too, and they're effective.
how: Attach small named bonuses to many kinds of actions so acknowledgment keeps coming.
example: Forza: bonuses for almost everything, including wrecking your car.
quote: And they're effective, so don't hold back on including them in your game.

title: The Family Computer (and the NES)
principle: Keep the original's game essence when moving to new hardware
why: Part of the Famicom's wonder was playing the arcade hit Donkey Kong at home with more or less the same game essence.
how: When porting or adapting a game, verify that the core play matches the original.
example: Donkey Kong on Famicom.
quote: You could even play the arcade hit Donkey Kong with more or less the same game essence.

title: Dying Comes as a Relief?
principle: Keep restarts quick so defeat never has time to sting
why: Whether the clock keeps running or a rematch begins, relatively quick restarts keep players pushing forward with no time to feel upset.
how: Minimize respawn and rematch delays and drop players straight back into play.
anti_pattern: Long post-death waits that let disappointment set in.
quote: as long as restart times are relatively quick, you can keep pushing forward— you won't have time to feel upset.

title: Dying Comes as a Relief?
principle: Design being defeated to be fun, not only defeating others
why: A study found competitive FPS players feel relief when defeated; when the fun of both defeating and being defeated clicks, there's no better entertainment.
how: Plan how each death motivates a retry, aiming for the reaction "I'll get you next time!"
anti_pattern: Assuming competitive fun is only the joy of dominating opponents.
example: Overseas study of competitive first-person shooter players.
quote: Remember, competitive games aren't only about the joy of dominating your opponent.

title: Dying Comes as a Relief?
principle: Account for the tension a non-decisive kill creates
why: The real objective is to win; if a kill doesn't settle the match it's too soon to relax, and it hints that you could be the next one defeated.
how: When tuning match flow, expect mid-match kills to raise the scorer's tension rather than relieve it.
quote: In a way, defeating an opponent shows you a potential future where you're the one defeated.

title: Mountain Climbing Is More Than Just Climbing
principle: Make bosses demand a strategy, then reward pulling it off
why: Bosses are the challenge peaks, and they shouldn't just be stronger versions of regular enemies.
how: Design each boss so players must form a strategy, and give a nice reward once they succeed.
anti_pattern: Bosses that are just beefed-up regular enemies.
quote: placing a boss should force the player to form a strategy, and once they're able to pull it off, they should get a nice reward for their trouble.

title: Make Retries Quick
principle: Minimize time from failure to regained control
why: Player interest cools quickly between thinking "I blew it" and getting control back; the longer the wait, the more they lose interest, while quick retries raise tolerance for difficulty.
how: Measure death-to-control time, trim the death presentation and load times, and hand control back immediately; if text must remain, let button presses advance it.
anti_pattern: Long death sequences, slow fades and loading screens before a retry.
quote: I'm talking about the time between when the player thinks, "Ugh, I blew it!" and when they actually get control again.

title: The Fun in Picking Sides
principle: Let spectators pick a side before the match starts
why: In a contest only one side can win, and having someone to root for makes it far more exciting; Smash's small point wagers work because they create investment, not because of the points.
how: Before a replay or spectated match, ask viewers to predict the winner with a small wager, and show identifying info about the players.
anti_pattern: Spectator modes that give viewers no stake in the outcome.
example: Super Smash Bros. online spectator mode with point wagers.
quote: In a contest between two sides where only one can win, you'll find yourself more fired up if you have someone to root for going in.

title: The Fun in Picking Sides
principle: Offer two or three meaningful choices instead of purely random draws
why: Choosing among a few draws, with a reason the choice carries weight, has more meaningful impact on players than pure randomness.
how: In gacha or random rewards, present 2-3 options and give each a reason that makes picking it matter.
anti_pattern: Purely random draws with no player choice.
example: Free-to-play gacha (his suggested application).

title: Is Your Game Appealing Enough to Start Over?
principle: Give players something they want to see next before forcing restarts
why: Most players won't enjoy repeating the same content endlessly; they continue out of a desire to see what comes next, so the game must show them something to look forward to.
how: Make upcoming content visible or hinted, and add variety (randomized equipment, items, events) to the repeated parts.
anti_pattern: Mimicking Souls-like or permadeath systems without creating the pull to push on.
example: Dark Souls players push on to reach what's next, partly from trust in FromSoftware.
quote: In other words, the game itself needs to be appealing enough to make players want to push on.

title: Game Essence in Shooting Games
principle: Make firepower depend on taking positional risks
why: Darius limits how many shots can be on screen, so hanging back uses up your shots while moving close lets you fire far more; staying back against bosses means less reward.
how: Cap on-screen player projectiles so effective fire rate rises as the player approaches enemies, and let aggressive positioning kill bosses faster.
anti_pattern: Letting the player easily wipe every enemy from safety, which has no push and pull.
example: Darius (Genesis version): shot limit, bombs and boss fights.

title: Game Essence in Shooting Games
principle: Give every weapon choice a real upside and downside
why: When each weapon has pros and cons, choosing one broadens the game essence; this kind of trade-off thinking works in any game.
how: Design options with explicit trade-offs (e.g., better upward coverage but only two shots at a time and weaker straight ahead).
example: Gradius: the double cannon vs. the laser.
quote: What downsides will you accept, and what upsides will you gain? I'd say this kind of thinking can be effective in any game.

title: Game Essence in Shooting Games
principle: Place rewards next to hazards
why: In Gradius, touching terrain costs a life, so enemies and power-ups placed beside terrain turn collecting them into a risk worth a reward.
how: Position power-ups and valuable targets near deadly geometry so getting them requires risk.
example: Gradius: power-ups near terrain.

title: Game Essence in Shooting Games
principle: Understand why a game is fun before borrowing from it
why: Mimicking an existing game won't give yours a unique flavor; and pushing game essence too hard can cost flair or make play a chore.
how: When studying a game you admire, write down the risk/reward structure that makes it fun, then design your own around that reason.
anti_pattern: Copying surface features of an existing game.
quote: don't just mimic an existing game. Instead, think about why that game is fun in the first place.

title: Knockback in Super Smash Bros.
principle: Make knockback grow with attack damage and the target's accumulated damage
why: In Smash, attacks don't just deplete health. Knockback is at the heart of the game's essence, so it must scale with both the hit and the target's state.
how: Compute launch strength from the attack's damage and the target's damage percentage, then adjust the arc by the target's weight and fall velocity.
anti_pattern: Treating attacks as simple health subtraction in a knockback-centered game.
example: Super Smash Bros. attack parameters, unchanged in structure since the original game.
quote: "Knockback" is at the heart of its game essence, so we have to make a few unique considerations.

title: More Game Essence Means Less Broad Appeal
principle: Scale reward with risk; accept that low risk means low thrill
why: Balanced correctly, risk and reward scale in almost perfect proportion: a more intense risk gives more intense joy, and low risk brings low reward.
how: When you lower risk for accessibility, expect less intense satisfaction and judge the design by whether it serves its audience.
anti_pattern: Expecting a low-risk game to be as thrilling as a high-risk one.
example: Kirby's Dream Land is less thrilling than Super Mario Bros., where you turn extreme risk next to enemies into a counterattack.
quote: Risk and reward, when balanced correctly, should scale in almost perfect proportion.

title: More Game Essence Means Less Broad Appeal
principle: Hold back rules that boost push and pull but hurt clarity
why: You can always add rules to increase game essence, but overcomplicated rulesets make the experience hard to grasp and reduce broad appeal.
how: Before adding a rule to deepen push and pull, check whether your target players could still grasp the game, and skip it if not.
anti_pattern: Piling on mechanics for depth until the game is hard to understand.
quote: Sometimes, it's important to hold back from a chance to boost game essence.

title: Special Crossover! #1
principle: Reward greed with bigger scores for chaining riskier plays
why: Several classic arcade games make the high-scoring play the dangerous one, so players are constantly tempted to push their luck.
how: Pay escalating points for chaining risky actions, such as eating several fleeing enemies in one power-up, clearing escorts before the leader, or crushing enemies with a dropped object.
anti_pattern: Making the safe play also the highest-scoring play.
example: Galaxian flagships worth more after escorts. Escalating points for fleeing blue ghosts. Crushing with rocks instead of inflating.
quote: It's really tempting to get greedy. After all, you get more points the more fleeing blue ghosts you can eat in one go.

title: Special Crossover! #1
principle: Let danger rise as a result of the player's own progress
why: In Space Invaders, the fewer invaders remain, the faster they move, so careless clearing lets them reach you quickly. Strategy emerges from that rule.
how: Tie enemy speed or aggression to how many threats remain, so the order of clearing becomes a strategic choice.
example: Space Invaders: clear one column at a time from the ends.
quote: Once you have fewer invaders to deal with, they'll move faster left and right

title: The Shoryuken Command
principle: Route your strongest reversal's input through the most vulnerable positions
why: The shoryuken's forward, down, down-forward command steps toward the opponent, drops guard against aerial attacks, then reaches the most dangerous stick position, so pulling it off turns vulnerability into an anti-air.
how: Design special-move inputs so that starting the input leaves the player exposed, making each attempt a gamble.
example: Street Fighter II — the shoryuken command
quote: In other words, this is the most dangerous stick position possible.

title: The Shoryuken Command
principle: Make reversal moves strongest when the opponent is closest
why: SFII's shoryuken is more powerful at its base and invincible at the start, so it is most effective the closer the opponent comes, exactly when you are most at risk of counterattack.
how: Give anti-air or reversal moves startup invincibility and peak damage at close range, and tune them alongside input difficulty, input time, opponent speed and miss punishment.
example: Street Fighter II — shoryuken strongest near its base, invincible at startup
quote: The closer they get, the greater the potential to turn things around— a perfect example of risk and reward philosophy.

title: The Shoryuken Command
principle: Scale each move's reward to the risk of using it
why: Sakurai feels SFII's heavy shoryuken, the riskiest variant, could have been even stronger, because a move with high risk should deliver a big reward.
how: When moves come in light, medium and heavy versions, make the riskiest one's payoff clearly the largest.
anti_pattern: Underpaying the riskiest option.
example: Street Fighter II — light, medium and heavy shoryuken
quote: A move with high risk should deliver a big reward.

title: The Pros and Cons of Leaderboards
principle: Link ranked results to an incentive to aim higher
why: Without a leaderboard you're just fighting and there's little thrill; it's vital that the result of hard work connects to a reason to push further.
how: Give competitive modes a visible standing that moves with performance so players have something to climb.
quote: It's vital that the result of your hard work is linked to an incentive to aim even higher.

title: What is “Play”?
principle: Let clever plays, not raw advantage, decide the winner
why: Game essence, or push and pull, is primarily agon (competition), and in Sakurai's view it is clever plays rather than physical advantage that should decide the victor.
how: Tune competitive mechanics so reads, timing and positioning can overcome stat or size advantages.
anti_pattern: Outcomes decided mainly by who has the bigger numbers.
quote: It's not simply physical advantage, but clever plays that decide the victor.

title: What is “Play”?
principle: Layer chance, imitation and vertigo onto your competitive core
why: Agon alone isn't all of play; alea, mimicry and ilinx each add a distinct kind of fun that Sakurai's games also rely on.
how: Audit your game for all four elements and add what's missing, such as randomly appearing items that can influence the outcome (alea).
example: Randomly appearing items in Sakurai's games influence the outcome.

title: Faithfulness Comes First in Licensed Games
principle: Put faithfulness to the source first in licensed games
why: Fans see the game as one form of a property among comics, anime, figures and events, and want faithfulness and their love satisfied more than great push and pull.
how: Set faithfulness as the top goal, then make the gameplay as fun as possible within it, and time the release alongside the property's other media.
anti_pattern: Freely changing the original's story and characters.
quote: It's product value versus fun. It's great if you can achieve both, but you'll never get a perfect score on all fronts.

title: Randomness Spices Games Up
principle: Use randomness to keep repeated play fresh and strategic
why: Games repeat the same content, and static rules struggle to deliver variety; randomness makes each play different and challenges players to handle a range of situations.
how: Vary probabilities instead of fixing results in places where repetition goes stale.

title: Game Essence in Action Games
principle: Give every core action both a danger and an opportunity
why: Game essence is taking risks and earning rewards, and in each action danger and opportunity are two sides of the same coin.
how: Pair benefits with costs: edge jumps clear more but risk falling, dashing is faster but harder to control or costs stamina, melee requires closing in.
anti_pattern: Actions whose benefit has no matching risk.

title: Game Essence in Action Games
principle: Pay for range and safety with resources or exposure
why: Unilateral attacks from afar would remove risk, so they need a cost.
how: Give longer-range weapons less ammo, let enemies shoot back, and make hiding limit your ability to attack.

title: Game Essence in Action Games
principle: Reward last-moment defensive timing heavily
why: Dodges and parries that work right before an attack lands let players turn massive risk into massive reward.
how: Make parries trigger only at the moment of impact with a big payoff, and give dodges a brief window where other actions are harder.
quote: By waiting until right when an attack is going to hit you, you can experience the fun of turning massive risk into massive reward.

title: Game Essence in Action Games
principle: Understand why a borrowed mechanic works before copying it
why: Considering the meaning behind each kind of game essence increases your chances of making something even more fun.
how: For each mechanic you borrow, write down its risk and reward and design your version from that reasoning.
anti_pattern: Mere imitation.
quote: Try to go beyond mere imitation!

title: Presenting Scores
principle: Express scores in a meaningful unit instead of bare points
why: Having something to strive for is what makes games fun; recasting the number as an age, money or power changes the game's meaning and makes the experience feel more real.
how: Pick a unit that fits your game's fantasy, such as Brain Age, Crash Dollars or Global Smash Power, and choose its direction (lower is better for an age).
anti_pattern: Dropping in a plain score counter without thinking about how it is presented.
example: Brain Age presents your score as your brain's age; Burnout's Crash Mode scores in Crash Dollars.
quote: The trick is that each variation is still based on a unit of measurement.

title: Making "Work" Games Fun
principle: Build a work-earn-upgrade loop first in task-based games
why: Working, earning money and then buying tools and skills that make the work easier gives work games their staying power; Sakurai calls it the first element to consider.
how: Make each job pay out currency that buys tools or skills which make the next job easier to finish.
anti_pattern: A work simulation with no profit or upgrade loop.
example: Car Mechanic Simulator, House Flipper and PowerWash Simulator all let you profit from the work.
quote: Without this loop, a game about work wouldn't have nearly as much staying power.

title: Making "Work" Games Fun
principle: Ground task games in real-world work so imagination fills gaps
why: With a real-world subject the player's mind fills in extra information, and striving toward the desired outcome keeps players doing the work.
how: Pick a recognizable job such as repair, renovation or cleaning, make the desired end result clear, and set the mood so players role-play the job.
example: House Flipper: cleaning up a room feels great, and a house can start to feel like your own home.

title: Average and Mediocre Are the Same Thing
principle: Pit distinct sides against each other for richer push and pull
why: Mirror matches like Mario vs. Mario remove balance issues but limit push and pull, while distinct sides create far more variety in strategy.
how: Give each character clear strengths and weaknesses so every matchup calls for different choices.
anti_pattern: Relying on identical sides to avoid balance problems.
example: Mario vs. Mario.
quote: Push and pull will still exist if both sides are identical, but there's a limit to how much.

title: Mandatory Strategies and Strategic Balance
principle: Decide deliberately between authored and free-form encounter strategies
why: Mandatory strategies show crafted thought but feel like tutorials, while free-form ones give freedom but can feel flavorless and create less push and pull; both are valid.
how: For each boss, decide up front whether it has one authored solution, an ideal strategy found by trial and error, or many viable weapon choices.
example: Nintendo bosses where you hit the eye and slash the stunned foe, compared with Castlevania's any-weapon freedom.
quote: Neither answer is more correct than the other, but you'll need to hone in on which experience you want.

title: Game Essence in Strategy Games
principle: Make mirror matches draw, then reward smarter army configuration
why: Identical armies must draw for the game to be fair, and the fun of strategy is changing your setup to beat an even opponent decisively.
how: Test mirror matchups for balance, then make sure composition choices clearly tip the outcome.
anti_pattern: A built-in advantage for one side.
example: Rock, Paper, Scissors: identical teams draw.
quote: Changing your configuration to achieve a crushing victory is the fundamental game essence found in strategy games.

title: Game Essence in Strategy Games
principle: Use attack range and position as a source of push and pull
why: In shogi and chess the push and pull comes from attack range, not strength, and long-range or map-based weapons make holding good positions the core.
how: Give units distinct ranges and make positioning matter as much as raw power.
example: Shogi and chess: tension comes from attack range and position.

title: How Good Were the Player’s Actions?
principle: Give slower, riskier attacks proportionally bigger payoffs
why: A move that takes time and leaves you open is harder to land, so landing it is more commendable and should pay off more.
how: Give high-startup, high-commitment moves more damage and knockback than quick, safe ones.
example: Smash Bros.: quick neutral attacks versus slow, vulnerable smash attacks with more damage and knockback.
quote: Landing a hit with the latter is a more commendable feat, so we've given it the damage and knockback such a feat deserves.

title: How Good Were the Player’s Actions?
principle: Break the reward rules deliberately with rare, hard-to-beat targets
why: Polishing every consequence can make a game predictable; an unusually lucrative enemy that is hard to beat becomes a special objective.
how: Add an occasional high-value enemy with high HP or a tendency to flee.

title: Turning Anything Into a Competitive Game
principle: Create competition by racing players through identical content simultaneously
why: Starting the same game at the same time turns even non-competitive games into contests, especially arcade games where one mistake ends your run.
how: Start both players together and decide the winner by first failure, higher score, progress or a set goal.
example: Sakurai and Arino Kacho started each game together in the Retro Game Master crossover.

title: Turning Anything Into a Competitive Game
principle: Show each player the opponent's progress to raise tension
why: A simple race gets heated when you can see how far your opponent has gotten.
how: Keep both screens or a progress indicator visible to both players in race or versus modes.
quote: It might seem simple, but things get pretty heated when you can see how far your opponent has gotten.

title: Amplify Both Strengths and Weaknesses
principle: Embrace divisive options that make players want to settle it in a match
why: If one player says A is better and another says B is better, the differences are fueling play; balance that isn't divisive would be the real problem. Social media echo chambers make this harder, but creators can't shy away.
how: Push the dynamic range between options as far as possible instead of sanding down whatever splits opinion.
anti_pattern: Backing away from distinctive designs because biases spread quickly on social media.
quote: You want those players to say: "Then let's settle it in a match!"
